title: Yara and the Colony
premise: Freya Dunmore has spent eleven years alone tending the Svalbard-adjacent Meridian Seed Vault, broadcasting maintenance logs to a colony on Kepler-44b that stopped answering years ago. When the deep-space vessel Halcyon returns carrying colonists who have aged backward into childhood due to a cryosleep temporal anomaly, Freya must become their reluctant guardian while Earth's dying reactor forces an impossible choice: wake only half of humanity's frozen gene bank, or let both halves die. As she falls in love with Idris, a returned colonist trapped between his adult memories and his child's body, she discovers her own logs were never transmissions—they were instructions she wrote to herself before a memory wipe. In the end, Freya sacrifices her restored identity to split the reactor's power, waking one half of humanity and preserving the seed vault for the other, choosing love and duty as two halves of the same act.
about_author: Mirabel Sterling is a former glaciologist who spent three winters at remote Arctic research stations before turning to fiction. She writes quiet, character-driven science fiction about people who keep the lights on at the edge of the world.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Establishes her solitary routine at the seed vault: cataloging seeds, logging reactor decay, sending daily reports to a colony that hasn't replied in four years. The emotional beat is loneliness worn smooth into ritual—she talks to the silence like it's listening.

chapters.title: A Light in the Ice
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A ship breaches the atmosphere—the Halcyon, presumed lost twelve years ago. She treks through the storm to the crash site and finds thirty children wearing the faces of adults she once knew. The beat is wonder curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Children of the Long Dark
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Idris, who remembers being forty but wakes at nine. The children struggle with fractured memories; Freya improvises caretaking. The beat is tender chaos—two kinds of brokenness recognizing each other.

chapters.title: What the Reactor Remembers
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. The reactor's countdown accelerates; there's power to wake either the cryo-bay's stored embryos or the vault's seed archive systems—not both. Idris, still a child, must translate adult engineering knowledge he can no longer perform. Beat: frustration and dawning responsibility.

chapters.title: The Logs That Lie
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Cross-referencing old records, she finds entries in her own handwriting from before her arrival—entries she doesn't remember writing, describing this exact crisis. The beat is vertigo: her identity as the forgotten caretaker begins to crack.

chapters.title: Half a Heart, Half a World
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Freya and Idris grow close—he remembers loving someone once, and it might be her. But duty pulls them apart: he argues for waking the children's future, she for the seeds that feed it. Beat: love against duty, made literal.

chapters.title: The Wipe
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She decodes her pre-wipe logs: she volunteered for memory erasure to test the cryo-temporal process that aged the Halcyon's crew backward—and it worked, which means reversal is possible. The beat is grief for a self she chose to lose.

chapters.title: Countdown
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. With hours left, the children vote on what to save—a haunting scene of small voices deciding humanity's future. Idris chooses to trust Freya over his own fragmented memories. Beat: surrender of ego to love.

chapters.title: Which Half Wakes
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, climax. She reroutes the reactor using herself as the biological key, restoring her full memories mid-process—remembering everything, including that the choice was always hers alone. She splits the power: half the embryos wake, the seed archive survives on minimal life support. Beat: sacrifice without martyrdom.

chapters.title: First Light, Second Spring
chapters.summary: Shared POV, resolution. Months later: the awakened colonists plant the first seeds beside the sleeping archive, and Freya—her past self and present self reconciled—writes a log entry meant to be read, not broadcast. Idris ages forward again, slowly. Beat: belonging found not in being remembered, but in choosing to stay.
